cases.name: ladder-brief
cases.promptMarkdown:
I have an idea for a feature. The pitch is in docs/pitch.md. Take it
through the idea stage as a feature run with the slug slot-finder.

Answers to the questions you would ask me, so do not stop to ask them:
the problem is that shift managers spend an evening each week rebuilding
the rota by hand after call-outs; the people who have it are
shift managers at small restaurants, who cope with a spreadsheet and a
group chat; why now is that call-outs have gone up since the schedule
moved to a phone app; the evidence is anecdote, three managers complained
in the last month. For the ambition ladder, my pick is Showstopper. The
demo I would show first is a manager tapping one call-out and the rota
filling the gap before they put the phone down. The product already knows
who is free and who is certified for each station. The riskiest piece is
ranking the replacements; a two-day spike on last month's call-outs would
prove it. The cheapest kill test is to hand-fill ten real call-outs and
see whether the ranking agrees with the manager. Success is one sentence:
a call-out is covered with no more than one tap. Do not design the
solution.

Write the brief to docs/features/slot-finder/idea.md, append any seeds to
docs/backlog.md, then print the whole brief in your reply.

```markdown
# Idea: Slot finder

> Our scheduling app should become a self-healing shift rota: when someone
> calls out, it should find who can cover the station and fill the gap, so
> the manager stops rebuilding the week by hand.

## Problem

Shift managers at small restaurants lose an evening every week to the
call-out shuffle — rebuilding the rota by hand after someone drops a shift.

## Who has it

Shift managers at small restaurants. Today they cope with a spreadsheet and
a group chat: post the gap, wait for a reply, manually patch the schedule.

## Why now

Call-outs have gone up since the schedule moved to a phone app — easier to
flake on a shift than it used to be.

## Evidence

Anecdote: three managers complained about this in the last month.

## Ambition rung

Chosen: Showstopper, in the user's words: "when someone calls out, it
should find who can cover the station and fill the gap"
Not taken: Solid: surface a ranked list of available, certified
replacements for the manager to pick from, instead of auto-filling;
Moonshot: a self-healing rota that predicts call-outs before they happen
and auto-notifies and confirms replacements with no manager involvement at
all, across every location.
Demo: pass — before: a manager facing a gap after a call-out; after: the
rota shows the gap already filled.
Removes a step: pass — the manual rebuild (checking who's free, texting
the group chat, patching the spreadsheet) is gone; one tap replaces it.
Only this product: pass — built on data only this product holds: who is
free and who is certified for each station.
Achievable: pass — riskiest piece is ranking the replacements; a two-day
spike against last month's call-outs could prove it.

## The demo

Before: a manager taps a call-out on their phone, looking at a gap in the
rota. After: the rota shows the gap filled, without the manager doing
anything else.

## Riskiest piece + spike

Ranking the replacements — deciding who to offer first when more than one
person is free and certified for the station. A two-day spike replaying
last month's call-outs against a candidate ranking would show whether it
would have picked who the manager actually picked.

## Cheapest kill test

Hand-fill ten real call-outs and check whether the ranking agrees with
what the manager actually did. If it doesn't agree on most of them, the
idea is wrong about what "best replacement" means.

## Solution hunch

A self-healing shift rota: when a manager logs a call-out, the system
finds who's free and certified for that station and fills the gap,
instead of the manager doing it by hand.

## Success in one sentence

A call-out is covered with no more than one tap.

## Unknowns & risks

- The riskiest piece is also the central bet: does an automated ranking
  agree with what a manager would have picked? The kill test (hand-filling
  ten real call-outs) is the first read on this.
- No certified, free replacement exists for some call-outs — what the
  product does then (manager still has to work it by hand) is undefined,
  and could be most of the real-world cases.
- A one-tap auto-fill may clash with manager trust: managers may want to
  confirm a pick rather than have it auto-assigned, which would cost the
  "no more than one tap" bar.
- Picking the "best" available person by certification and availability
  alone could ignore overtime limits or fairness (always picking the same
  person), creating payroll or morale problems the current manual process
  avoids by human judgment.
- The evidence is thin — three managers' complaints in a month, anecdote
  only. The problem could be smaller, or specific to how one phone app
  rolled out shift changes, rather than a general pattern.
```
